newsitem.title: GERMANY: Chirpy German Bund futures set sights on 103.00.
newsitem.headline: Chirpy German Bund futures set sights on 103.00.

text.p: German Bunds and futures stretched to dizzy heights on Monday with the September DTB future plotting a new contract high at 102.92 in late trade.
Dealers said debt prices were benefiting mainly from a positive technical bachground, but were also helped by a slightly stronger mark exchange rate versus the dollar.
"I'm not suprised to see prices going this high," said one futures broker in London. "The technicals are very good at the moment and people are keen to go long."
By 1441 GMT, the September Bund future was 43 basis points higher at 102.85, just below the contract peak at 102.92.

Analysts said that after the futures contract broke above a key barrier at 102.59, fresh buyers were tempted into the market. The contract should now overcome further interim hurdles and head for 103.00 in the near term, they said.
"The 75 percent swing from 100.94 of the 99.32 to 101.88 move at 102.86 is now the intervening resistance barrier ahead of 103.00," said one Frankfurt-based analyst.
Looking at continuation charts, the DTB Bund futures have not seen levels as high as 103.00 since March 5, when the market broke down from a high at 103.29 to end the day's trade at 102.60.
But traders warned that this session's rally might not be as reliable as some of the upmoves from last week, since trading volumes were light.
"The markets (in Europe) are all looking pretty okay, but we have to remember that the volume in Bunds has been quite thin today," said one.

In the cash market, the 10-year benchmark Bund was quoted at 103.38 for a 5.542 percent bid yield by 1456 GMT, while the yield spread to the corresponding U.S. T-note widened slightly to 82 basis points from 80 basis points at Friday's close. The market's main focus on Tuesday will be unemployment.

Analysts said rumours in the market suggested jobless numbers for June should be broadly in line with expectations and will serve mainly to maintain the current view that both inflation and interest rates will remain capped for the time being.
EMU worries will also continue to be of interest with German Finance Minister Theo Waigel due to present a supplementary 1997 budget, as well as the 1998 budegt proposal, to the cabinet on Friday.
